title: Chapter 29 — Enter Ahab; to Him, Stubb
paragraphs: Some days passed. With ice and icebergs all behind us, the Pequod now rolled through the bright spring of the equatorial regions, which at sea reigns almost perpetually on the threshold of the eternal summer of the Tropics. The warm yet cool, clear, ringing, fragrant, overflowing days were like crystal goblets of Persian sherbet, heaped up and flaked with rose-water snow. The starry, stately nights seemed like proud ladies in jeweled velvet, nursing at home in lonely pride the memory of their absent conquering lords, the golden-helmeted suns! For a sleeping man, it was hard to choose between such enchanting days and such seductive nights. But all the magic of that endless fair weather didn't just add new spells to the outer world. It worked inward upon the soul too, especially during the mild evening hours, when memory formed its crystals like clear ice in the noiseless twilight. And all these subtle forces worked more and more on Ahab's nature.

Old age is always wakeful, as if the longer a man is linked with life, the less he wants anything to do with what resembles death. Among sea captains, the old graybeards are the ones who most often leave their beds to visit the night-wrapped deck. So it was with Ahab, except that lately he seemed to live so much in the open air that, truly speaking, his visits were more to the cabin than from it. "It feels like going down into one's tomb," he would mutter to himself, "for an old captain like me to be descending this narrow hatch to my grave-dug bed."

So almost every twenty-four hours, when the night watches were set and the men on deck guarded the sleep of those below — when if a rope needed hauling on the forecastle, the sailors dropped it gently to its place rather than flinging it down, for fear of waking their shipmates — when this sort of steady quiet would settle in, the silent helmsman would watch the cabin hatch, and before long the old man would emerge, gripping the iron railing to help his crippled way. There was some touch of human consideration in him. At times like these, he usually avoided pacing the quarter-deck, because to his exhausted mates, trying to sleep within six inches of his ivory heel, the reverberating crack of that bony step would have filled their dreams with the crunching teeth of sharks. But once, his mood ran too deep for such consideration. As he paced the ship with a heavy, lumbering stride from stern to mainmast, Stubb, the old second mate, came up from below. With a certain uneasy, apologetic humor, he suggested that if Captain Ahab was pleased to walk the planks, then no one could argue. But there might be some way of muffling the noise — hinting vaguely and hesitantly about a ball of rope fiber and inserting it around the ivory heel. Ah, Stubb! You didn't know Ahab then.

"Am I a cannonball, Stubb," said Ahab, "that you'd want to pad me like that? But go your way — I forgot. Down to your nightly grave, where the likes of you sleep wrapped in shrouds, getting used to the one you'll fill at last. Down, dog, and to your kennel!"

Startled by this unexpected, suddenly scornful outburst from the old man, Stubb was speechless for a moment. Then he said with agitation, "I'm not used to being spoken to that way, sir. I don't half like it, sir."
"Enough!" Ahab growled through clenched teeth, moving violently away as if to avoid some passionate temptation.
"No, sir, not yet," said Stubb, growing bolder. "I won't meekly accept being called a dog, sir."
"Then be called ten times a donkey, and a mule, and an ass, and get out of my sight, or I'll rid the world of you!"
As he said this, Ahab advanced on him with such overpowering menace in his bearing that Stubb involuntarily backed away.

"I was never treated like that without throwing a punch for it," Stubb muttered as he found himself going down the cabin hatch. "This is very strange. Stop, Stubb. Somehow, I don't quite know whether to go back and hit him, or — what's that? — get down here on my knees and pray for him? Yes, that was the thought rising up in me. But it would be the first time I ever prayed. It's strange. Very strange. And he's strange too. Take him front to back, he's about the strangest old man Stubb ever sailed with. How he flashed at me! His eyes like gunpowder! Is he mad? Either way, there's something on his mind, as sure as there must be something on a deck when it cracks. He doesn't sleep in his bed more than three hours out of twenty-four, and he doesn't really sleep even then. Didn't Dough-Boy, the steward, tell me that every morning the old man's hammock is all rumpled and twisted, sheets kicked to the foot, covers nearly tied in knots, and the pillow frightfully hot, as though a baked brick had been on it? A restless old man! I guess he's got what some folks ashore call a conscience — a kind of torture, they say — worse than a toothache. Well, well, I don't know what it is, but the Lord keep me from catching it. He's full of riddles. I wonder what he goes into the aft hold for every night, as Dough-Boy suspects. What's that about? Who's he meeting in the hold? Isn't that strange? But there's no telling — it's the same old game. Time for a nap. Damn me, it's worth being born just to fall right asleep. And now that I think about it, that's about the first thing babies do, and that's sort of strange too. Damn me, but everything's strange when you think about it. But that's against my principles. Don't think — that's my eleventh commandment. And sleep when you can — that's my twelfth. So here goes again. But wait — didn't he call me a dog? Blazes! He called me ten times a donkey, and piled a load of jackasses on top of that! He might as well have kicked me and been done with it. Maybe he did kick me, and I didn't notice — I was so stunned by that brow of his. It flashed like bleached bone. What the devil's wrong with me? I don't feel steady on my legs. Running into that old man has sort of turned me inside out. By the Lord, I must have been dreaming — how? how? how? But the only thing to do is forget it. So back to the hammock, and in the morning I'll see how this damned puzzle looks by daylight."
